title: 3-Read Friday #119
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's weekly '3-Read Friday' curates three education blog posts worth a teacher's attention, and issue #119 gathers a strong trio on assessment proxies, task design, and maths resources. The lead item is David Didau's 'Why I hate beautiful books,' which Barton connects to his own earlier argument ('The Myth of Copying Things Down') that neat exercise books are a poor proxy for understanding — Didau's point being that once leaders signal what they want to see, teachers rationally perform to it, so neat pages can conceal shallow thinking while scruffy ones may hold real intellectual graft. The second is Michael Pershan's study of how Henri Picciotto designs great classroom activities, which Barton frames as essential reading for anyone interested in task design: the 'quiet genius' lies in a single set of instructions that still generates rich mathematics, a deliberate stance between open exploration and explicit teaching, and a practising teacher's eye for what actually works with real students. The third is Jo Morgan's milestone '5 Maths Gems #200,' a browse-and-grab roundup of practical classroom tools — self-testing key-facts sheets, a new graphing tool, the now-complete NCETM Key Stage 4 mastery materials, and self-marking worksheet sites. As a curated digest, its archival value is the selection judgement and editorial framing Barton brings, pointing teachers toward the specific ideas in each linked piece.
points: The curation's throughline is a healthy scepticism about proxies for learning: Didau's 'beautiful books' critique and Barton's own 'Myth of Copying Things Down' both warn that visible neatness is rewarded even though it can mask shallow thinking — a caution for any leader designing book scrutiny or work-sampling routines.

Pershan-on-Picciotto is flagged as a task-design masterclass: the design principles — one instruction set that still yields rich mathematics, a stance poised between open exploration and explicit teaching, and a practitioner's eye for what works with real pupils — are transferable criteria for evaluating or building classroom activities.

Jo Morgan's 'Maths Gems #200' is positioned as a practical resource haul (self-testing key-facts sheets, a graphing tool, completed NCETM KS4 mastery materials, self-marking worksheet sites) — a 'browse-and-grab' post whose value is immediate classroom applicability rather than argument.

As a Pass-A roundup, the issue's independent worth is editorial: Barton's selection and framing tell a teacher not just what to read but why each piece matters, connecting new posts to a longer conversation about assessment and design.
quotes: David argues that the moment leaders signal what they want to see, teachers rationally perform to it. Neat pages can conceal shallow thinking; scruffy ones can hold hard graft.
In that post, I made the point that neat books are a poor proxy for understanding. David articulates this point, and much more, beautifully.

Michael argues that the quiet genius of Henri’s activities lies in three design choices — a single set of instructions that still generates rich mathematics, a stance poised between open exploration and explicit teaching, and a practising teacher’s eye for what genuinely works with real students.
Anyone who spends time thinking about task design will love this closer look at what makes a resource actually work in a classroom. The examples are where it clicks.
A milestone edition from one of the most reliably useful maths blogs going — 200 gems posts is a staggering run, and this one’s as generous as ever.

Jo rounds up her latest haul for maths teachers — self-testing key-facts sheets, a slick new graphing tool, the finally-complete NCETM Key Stage 4 mastery materials, and a couple of self-marking worksheet sites worth a look.
